Dear Esteemed Jurors,

I am not the owner of this profile. I am writing to support the submitter. I have read the challenge. I believe the Juror should vote YES.

 An “Incorrect Submission” challenge is only for a real broken rule. The policy gives clear examples of a real broken rule: a mirrored photo, a hateful name, or using the same old video again. The policy says the photo must face the camera and sit the right way so the face can be recognised. That is the job of the photo: so people can tell who the person is. The same face is in the photo and in the video, and the video shows him holding the address. If jurors can tell it is the same living person, the photo has done its job. The policy does not use extra photo tests beyond that.

For these two reasons, the challenge is not valid. Please vote YES.

evidenceJSON.name: A supporting defense against the claims of wrong submission
evidenceJSON.description:
Good day, Jurors.

I would like to add in defense against the challenger’s claim of wrong submission that the policy’s lighting requirement does not state that every individual component of the eyes, such as the iris or pupil, must be separately discernible. Instead, for video submissions, it states that “Lighting conditions and recording device quality must be sufficient to discern internal facial features.” Therefore, the supposed question under the policy is whether the internal facial features, including the eyes, are sufficiently visible to be discerned, not whether the iris and pupil satisfy an additional standard that is not expressly provided in the policy. The required conditions were clearly met in his submission.

In my opinion, this claim of wrong submission should be rejected and be judged accordingly to the exact rule guiding the proof of humanity.

And a YES vote should be given on this judgement.

Just my own opinion.

evidenceJSON.title: Challenge Justification
evidenceJSON.description:
The token name is not SODA; it's SODAX. I will prove this with 3 pieces of evidence, each with its own evidence post, to make it easier to follow.
Firstly, by going to this block explorer detail page associated with the submitted token contract: https://snowscan.xyz/address/0x390ceed555905ec225da330a188ea04e85570f00, under the "Token Tracker" info section, "SODAX (SODA)" is observed (Shown in the attached screenshot). This particular explorer (i.e., Snowscan) and many others usually follow a token naming format, which is the token name, followed by a space, and then the token symbol or ticker in parentheses (i.e. "Token Name (Token Symbol/Ticker)" ).  All ERC20 tokens follow this naming format on this explorer. For example, under the "Token Tracker" section on the associated explorer detail page for the Tether token (i.e. https://snowscan.xyz/address/0x9702230A8Ea53601f5cD2dc00fDBc13d4dF4A8c7) is TetherToken (USDt), where "TetherToken" is the token name and "USDT" is the token symbol/ticker. So, following this token naming format, the token name for the submitted token contract would be "SODAX", not SODA.

evidenceJSON.title: 2nd Evidence
evidenceJSON.description: By navigating to the read contract section on an Avalanche C-Chain block explorer detail page associated with the submitted token contract, you could verify its token name and token symbol/ticker. The token contract is unverified on Snowscan.xyz, so we would be using dedaub.com, a very reputable contract decompilation platform,  to decompile the contract so that we can read its contract information. By navigating to the read contract section on the link generated after the token contract has been decompiled (i.e. https://app.dedaub.com/avalanche/address/0x390ceed555905ec225da330a188ea04e85570f00/read). You would note that the value under the "name" field shows "SODAX", while the value under the "symbol" field is "SODA" (Shown in the attached screenshot). So, the token name is "SODAX", not "SODA", as verified.

evidenceJSON.title: 3rd Evidence
evidenceJSON.description:
Finally, I verified with the SODAX team on Discord (i.e. https://discord.com/invite/xM2Nh4S6vN) what the token name and symbol are. They said, "fyi the asset is SODAX and the ticker is SODA" (Shown in the attached screenshot). In the context of crypto tokens, a token ticker is the same as its token symbol, and the asset is the same as the token itself, whose name is SODAX. Also, since they explicitly state that the token ticker/symbol is "SODA", the token name can't also be "SODA". This verifies the token name is indeed "SODAX", not "SODA". 

The submitter must have been confused due to the ticker or symbol "SODA" being used extensively on the tokenomics page here: https://www.sodax.com/holders/soda-token. This is similar to "USDT" being extensively used on the tokenomics page and confusing for its token name, "Tether".

evidenceJSON.title: JURORS PLEASE READ
evidenceJSON.description: The challenge conflates the protocol name with the token name. On SODAX’s official website (https://www.sodax.com/holders/soda-token), the page is explicitly titled “SODA Token” and states: “SODA is the fixed supply asset…” and “SODA is a native token…”. The attached screenshot also shows the official navigation labels “SODA Token”, “Buy SODA” and “SODA Tokenomics”. The same page separately describes “SODAX” as the cross-network execution and liquidity system, clearly distinguishing SODAX (protocol) from SODA (token). Explorer/decompiler metadata showing name() = SODAX does not erase the project’s own first-party naming. Likewise, the Discord wording only shows inconsistent terminology, not that “SODA” is invalid. Since the official issuer repeatedly identifies the token as SODA, the submission is supported by direct first-party evidence and should not be rejected.

evidenceJSON.title: OFFICIAL TOKEN NAME
evidenceJSON.description:
Part 2 – Policy

THE POLICIES NAME directly supports the submission: “If there is more than one official name, any of them is acceptable, except in the case of a rebranding.” Here, SODA is clearly used as an official token name by the project itself on its official website, including the explicit labels “SODA Token” and “SODA Tokenomics.” Therefore, even if “SODAX” is also considered an official name based on the contract metadata, the policy expressly states that any official name must be accepted. There is no evidence of a rebranding from SODA to SODAX. Accordingly, the existence of “SODAX” does not invalidate the submitted name SODA, and the challenge should be rejected.

THE TOKEN HAS TO BE ACCEPTED.

evidenceJSON.title: Part 3  .... Official Brand Kit
evidenceJSON.description: Further first-party evidence comes from SODAX’s official brand kit. After downloading the “SODAX-brand-kit”, there is a dedicated folder named “Token”, and the files inside are explicitly named “Soda token.” This is significant because the brand kit is the project’s own official branding material, specifically intended to define how its protocol, logos, symbol, and token should be identified. The fact that the token assets themselves are labeled “Soda token” independently confirms that SODA is an official name used by the SODAX team for the token, further supporting the submission and contradicting the claim that the token can only be named “SODAX.”

evidenceJSON.title: Part 4 – Official SODAX Help Center
evidenceJSON.description: SODAX’s official Help Center provides an explicit clarification of the naming. When asked whether the correct name is SODA ($SODA) or SODAX $SODA, its support AI responded: “SODA → the token,” “$SODA → the token symbol,” and “SODAX → the project/protocol.” It further states that the normal format is “SODA ($SODA)” and summarizes: “SODAX = project” and “SODA / $SODA = token.” This directly addresses the challenger’s argument: SODAX identifies the project/protocol, while SODA is the token name and $SODA its symbol. This is fully consistent with the official website, the “SODA Token” navigation, and the project’s official brand kit.

evidenceJSON.title: Team confirms explicitly that the token name is SODAX
evidenceJSON.description: I'm not conflating the token name and the project name. All 3 pieces of evidence point to "SODAX" being the token name. A SODAX team member on Discord explicitly states that the asset/token name is SODAX and the ticker/symbol is SODA. An official confirmation like this should be enough to clear all doubts.  The official confirmation doesn't include another name (e.g. SODA) for the token as stated by the submitter.  A lot of projects tend to use more of the token ticker/symbol to refer to their tokens on their platform; that doesn't mean it is the token name.  For example, USD Coin (USDC) refer to its token using its ticker "USDC" on the homepage of its website (i.e. https://www.usdc.com/?r=0), instead of its token name, "USD Coin". The same is true for Synthetix's Synthetix Network Token (SNX) here: https://sips.synthetix.io/sips/sip-315/, where the token ticker, SNX, is used extensively. The fact that the ticker is used extensively in both examples doesn't automatically make them token names. And AIs are generally known for being quite unreliable when fact-checking; it's usually best to confirm with the project team. The official confirmation of which I got from Discord.

evidenceJSON.title: Direct Confirmation from a Team Member that the name is SODA
evidenceJSON.description:
To remove any remaining doubt, I took the time to contact an actual member of the team directly, instead of relying on the AI support agent.

 I explicitly asked whether the correct token name is SODA ($SODA), and the team member confirmed it twice: “It’s SODA” and “Correct, it’s SODA.”

This is direct first-party confirmation from someone on the team that SODA is the token name and $SODA is its ticker/symbol. Together with the official website, brand kit, and the applicable naming policy, this further confirms that SODA is a valid official name. 

Therefore, the challenge should be rejected. 

Vote YES ADD IT.

evidenceJSON.title: Core Team member vs ad hoc staff member confirmation
evidenceJSON.description:
Lol, it's very interesting that we have 2 different confirmations from the team. The support (i.e. Hazy)  that the submitter got his confirmation from seems to think that "$" in "$SODA" indicates a hashtag on social media. Hazy doesn't even know that, in the context of crypto tokens, it denotes a token's ticker symbol. This alone makes any confirmation given by this particular support  (i.e. Hazy) regarding tokens questionable.

Also, Hazy is not an 'actual' team member; he is simply a freelance community manager/support  whom the actual SODAX team members hired to handle support/community management of their platforms. He is simply an external party on a contract job. This is shown in the attached screenshot of the joined Hazy's and John's SODAX Discord server profiles. While it's clearly shown that John, who confirmed that SODAX is the token name, is an actual team member, as his profile has the "SODAX Team" role. Hazy is shown to be just a community manager/support, as no "SODAX Team" role can be seen on his profile. Also, going to Hazy's personal link shown on his Discord profile (i.e. https://hasantoprak.xyz/), you would see he does community management/support as a business for multiple projects. He is currently hired as a community manager for about 3 different projects aside from SODAX. So, how is he a team member? At best, he is an ad hoc staff member. That would explain the incorrect and surface-level confirmation he gave the submitter

So, jurors, which of the confirmations would you rather regard as valid? Is it the confirmation from a core team member that most likely knows the SODAX project thoroughly, or the confirmation from some freelancer that just happened to get hired by the actual team members and likely has a surface-level knowledge of the SODAX project compared to the actual team?

evidenceJSON.title: Token name on CoinMarketCap is SODAX.
evidenceJSON.description:
CoinMarketCap, a very reputable crypto token tracking platform, shows the token name as "SODAX" and the token ticker/symbol as "SODA", as seen here: https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/sodax/.

Tokens published on CoinMarketCap are usually listed by their owners, so it's safe to say that the SODAX team themselves listed the SODAX token on CoinMarketCap.

evidenceJSON.title: SODA IS CONFIRMED BY official SOURCES
evidenceJSON.description:
The evidence already confirms that SODA is the official token name and $SODA is its ticker/symbol. This is supported by multiple first-party sources: the official website uses “SODA Token” and “SODA Tokenomics”; the official brand kit includes files named “Soda token”; the project’s official support AI confirmed SODA = token and $SODA = symbol; and a human representative of the project independently confirmed twice that the correct token is SODA / $SODA.

Most importantly, the policy states:

“IF THERE IS MORE THAN ONE OFFICIAL NAME, ANY OF THEM IS ACCEPTABLE, EXCEPT IN THE CASE OF A REBRANDING.”

Therefore, even if another source uses a different naming convention, that does not invalidate SODA, which is clearly supported by official project-controlled evidence. 

The challenge should be rejected AND THE TOKEN HAS TO BE ADD IT TO THE LIST.
